title: Which side of the plane should you sit on flying to Gran Canaria?
author: Brogan
intro: Flying into Gran Canaria from the UK, the left side of the plane usually gets the best view of the island as you land, with the east coast, the mountains behind it and, on some approaches, the south of the island. Here's why, when it changes and which seats to pick.
seo_title: Flying to Gran Canaria: sit on the left (usually)
seo_description: Usually the left side (seat A) for the island and mountains as you land at Gran Canaria. Why the trade winds decide it, when it flips, and flying home.

sections.heading: The short answer
sections.text:
- **Best side:** left, seat A
- **Why:** landings usually head north
- **When it flips:** on rare south-west winds
- **Flight time:** about 4 to 4½ hrs

This is guidance, not a guarantee. The wind decides which way planes land, and air traffic control decides the exact route in, so no seat is certain. But on most days the odds are on the left.

sections.heading: Why the left side usually wins
sections.text:
Gran Canaria's airport is on the island's east coast, between Las Palmas in the north and the big resorts of Maspalomas and Playa del Inglés in the south. Its two parallel runways run roughly south-south-west to north-north-east, close to the shore. The Canary Islands sit in the north-east trade winds, and planes land into the wind. So on most days, aircraft land on the runway pointing north-east, known as runway 03, which means the final approach comes up from the south over the sea, heading north.

On that final approach, the island is on your **left** and the open Atlantic is on your right. From an A seat you may see the east coast towns, the dry ravines running down from the mountains and, on a clear day, the peaks of the interior behind them.

Tip: arrivals from the north often fly down past the island first and turn back to line up with the runway. If your route swings round the south, the left side may also get a look at the dunes at Maspalomas.

sections.heading: How the approach usually works
sections.text:
| Wind | Runway used | Best side for the island |
| --- | --- | --- |
| North-east trade winds (most days) | 03, landing heading north | left (seat A) |
| South-westerly (uncommon) | 21, landing heading south | right (seat F) |
| Light or changing winds | either | left is still the better bet |

Whichever runway is in use, the earlier part of the descent varies from day to day. Depending on how you're brought round to line up with the runway, you might see parts of the island from either side, so a window on either side beats an aisle seat.

sections.heading: Which seats to choose
sections.text:
Where you sit along the plane matters almost as much as the side:

- **In front of the wing** gives the clearest view, but those rows often cost more to choose.
- **Behind the wing** is usually the best value, with a clear view down as the plane descends.
- **Over the wing**, the wing and engine block most of the view below.
- **Check the seat map:** some window seats on popular jets don't line up with a window at all.

On a Boeing 737 or Airbus A320, which most airlines use for Gran Canaria, the left window seat is **A** and the right is **F**. If your airline assigns seats for free at check-in, paying to choose is the only way to be sure of a left-side window.

sections.heading: On the way home
sections.text:
Most departures take off towards the north-east, into the wind, along the coast. Planes then turn north for the UK.

On take-off the island is again on the **left**, with Las Palmas and the north-east coast below as you climb. After that, which side gets the view depends on the turn, so it varies.

Watch out: on afternoon flights home, the sun is often on the left side of the plane for much of the trip, so a right-hand seat can be more comfortable if you want to sleep or read.

sections.heading: What you might see
sections.text:
Gran Canaria is sometimes called a continent in miniature, and it shows from the air. On a clear day you might spot:

- **The Maspalomas dunes**, a sweep of golden sand at the southern tip of the island.
- **The central mountains**, including Roque Nublo and Pico de las Nieves, often above a band of cloud.
- **Las Palmas**, the island's capital, and Las Canteras beach in the north.
- **Tenerife's Teide**, the snow-capped volcano on the next island to the west, which can sometimes be seen above the clouds.

The flight from most UK airports takes around four to four and a half hours, so there's plenty of time to read up before you land.

sections.heading: Planning a trip to Gran Canaria?
sections.text:
Our [Gran Canaria guide](/destinations/gran-canaria) covers when to go, how long to stay and what to see. If you're deciding between islands, our [Gran Canaria or Tenerife](/blog/gran-canaria-or-tenerife) post compares the two biggest, and [is Gran Canaria warm in December?](/blog/is-gran-canaria-warm-in-december) covers the winter weather.

Flying somewhere else in the Canaries? See which side to sit on flying to [Tenerife](/blog/which-side-of-the-plane-to-sit-on-flying-to-tenerife) or [Lanzarote](/blog/which-side-of-the-plane-to-sit-on-flying-to-lanzarote), or our general guide to [which side of the plane to sit on](/blog/which-side-of-the-plane-to-sit-on).

faqs.question: Which side of the plane is best for landing in Gran Canaria?
faqs.answer: Usually the left side, seat A on most holiday jets. Planes normally land heading north into the trade winds, with the island on the left and the sea on the right.

faqs.question: Can you see the Maspalomas dunes from the plane?
faqs.answer: Sometimes. If your approach swings round the south of the island before landing, the dunes are usually on the left. It depends on the route air traffic control gives on the day.

faqs.question: How long is the flight to Gran Canaria from the UK?
faqs.answer: About four to four and a half hours from most UK airports, a little longer from Scotland.

faqs.question: Can you see Tenerife from the plane to Gran Canaria?
faqs.answer: On clear days you can sometimes see Teide, Tenerife's volcano, to the west. It's often snow-capped in winter and can stand out above the clouds.
